newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU still wheat seller at right price, official say.
newsitem.headline: EU still wheat seller at right price, official say.

text.p: The European Union remains a seller of wheat on the world market but volumes between now and the end of the season will depend strictly on bids at its weekly tender, an EU grain official said on Thursday.

"It is important to show we are selling, that we remain a reliable origin," the official said, adding that a new buying tender from Tunisia illustrated there was still new business coming in from the EU's traditional outlets.
But the official warned that the Commission, though cautious on budgets this year, would not get involved in a downward spiral of refunds caused by speculation on export licences.
"We are a seller but at the normal price of the tender. We will especially not reward companies which are not paying attention to our regular customers," he said.

A net shortage of export licences put at 500,000 tonnes has been pushing down EU refunds as exporters try to cover loss-making sales, while one company has been accused of worsening the problem by carrying out a squeeze on licences.
The EU eased the situation last week by putting the cut-off for refunds higher than several traders had expected.

Tension surfaced again this week after a European Commission official said the EU could not continue giving out licences at the current weekly rate of 400,000 tonnes right up to the end of April, which usually marks the final stage of the campaign. Doing so would imply further sales of 2.4 million tonnes.

EU analysts said the prediction tallied with remaining EU export prospects closer to 1.0-1.5 million tonnes, but was not designed to send a negative signal to the market. The EU has released 8.1 million tonnes of commercial soft wheat for export since the crop year began on July 1, 1996.
The EU official on Thursday reiterated Brussels had started the season with an informal export goal of 8.0 to 9.0 million tonnes and said this target appeared easily achievable.

Combined with high internal consumption, caused by plentiful feed wheat and high soybean prices, earlier forecasts of three to four million tonnes being left behind in EU storage may now be too high, he said.
"It looks as though we may be able to end the season with quite a modest build-up in intervention," he said.
That will provide cost savings to the Commission, where the cost to the central EU farm budget of funding intervention storage can add up to 20 to 25 Ecus a tonne over a full year.
On barley, the EU has a remaining export potential of around one million tonnes this season, the EU official said.
Traders are still waiting for confirmation that Saudi Arabia may buy as much as that amount some time in late April. One trade source said a purchase was now unlikely before May 1.
Iran meanwhile said it would tender on March 17 for 50,000 tonnes of optional-origin barley. It also wants barley under a relief operation for its quake-stricken region in the northwest.
